Female snoek (Thyrsites atun) achieve a remarkable ultimate total length of 200 centimetres [Li = 200 centimetres], placing them among the larger members of the Gempylidae family. This impressive size is accompanied by a correspondingly high asymptotic wet weight, with the heaviest individuals recorded at approximately 9000 grams [Wwi = approximately 9000 grams], a mass that reflects the substantial somatic investment required to sustain a piscivorous, pelagic lifestyle in the cool, productive waters of the Southern Hemisphere. In contrast to this considerable adult mass, the species begins life as a minute, pelagic larva emerging from a small, buoyant egg. The initial wet weight at birth, based on the size of the fertilised ovum, is an exceptionally low 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams], a value that underscores the extreme fecundity and high larval mortality typical of many marine teleosts. Growth from this near-infinitesimal starting point to a multi-kilogram adult represents a dramatic ontogenetic trajectory spanning several orders of magnitude in body mass.

The onset of reproductive capability in snoek is tied to the attainment of a specific body size rather than a strict chronological age. Sexual maturation, defined by the initiation of gametogenesis, occurs when females reach a total length of 73 centimetres [Lp = 73 centimetres], a measurement reported by Griffiths in 2002 based on fork length equivalents. At this size, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is 437 grams [Wwp = 437 grams], a value derived from the allometric relationship between length and mass for this species. This relatively modest size at puberty, compared to the ultimate adult length, suggests a life-history strategy in which individuals begin reproducing while still capable of considerable further somatic growth, an iteroparous pattern typical of many long-lived predatory fishes. Reaching this developmental milestone allows individuals to enter the spawning population and contribute to the next generation before achieving their full asymptotic dimensions.

At a water temperature of 11.2 °C [T = 11.2 °C], snoek exhibit a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 9% [GSI = 9%]. Field surveys conducted in the Benguela Current ecosystem have confirmed that spawning activity peaks during the austral winter, aligning with the thermal optimum that appears to regulate several key life-history processes in this species.

At a temperature of 11.2 °C [T = 11.2 °C], the incubation period from egg fertilisation to chorion rupture lasts approximately 6 days [ab = approximately 6 days], a relatively rapid eclosion time for a pelagic egg of its size. This brief embryonic phase suggests that yolk reserves are consumed efficiently to support the rapid differentiation of larval structures necessary for the transition to exogenous feeding. Following hatching, the yolk-sac larva remains endotrophic for a short period before the mouth opens and first exogenous feeding begins, a trophic switch that must occur within a narrow window to avoid starvation mortality. The prolonged lifespan of the species, however, ensures that even with high larval mortality, sufficient recruits survive to maintain the population. The maximum longevity recorded for snoek in the wild is approximately 3650 days [am = approximately 3650 days], equivalent to a decade of life, which was also documented at the same ambient thermal regime at a temperature of 11.2 °C [T = 11.2 °C].

This decade-long maximum lifespan of roughly 3650 days [am = roughly 3650 days] places snoek among the longer-lived members of its family and implies a life-history strategy built around moderate adult mortality and sustained reproductive output over many years at a temperature of 11.2 °C [T = 11.2 °C]. The combination of a relatively early puberty at 73 centimetres [Lp = 73 centimetres] total length and a substantial ultimate adult mass of 9000 grams [Wwi = 9000 grams] suggests that females can partition energy between continued somatic growth and annual reproductive effort across their adult lives. The wet weight at birth of only 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams] and the six-day incubation period (6 days) [ab = 6 days] together highlight a strategy reliant on high fecundity and rapid early development rather than large egg size or prolonged maternal investment at a temperature of 11.2 °C [T = 11.2 °C]. Comparative data from other temperate gempylids indicate that this suite of traits — small eggs, rapid hatching, early maturation at a moderate size, and a multi-decadal lifespan — is well suited to the variable but productive upwelling ecosystems that snoek inhabits.
